item.title: The Hollowed-Out Downtown: How Remote Work Rewrote the Math of America's Office Market
item.body:
For most of the postwar era, the American downtown ran on a simple assumption: companies would keep needing more desks, and those desks would keep being downtown. Cities built their tax bases, transit systems, and street-level economies on that assumption. Investors underwrote billions of dollars in office towers on it.

That assumption broke in 2020, and — unlike the temporary shocks of previous recessions — it never fully repaired itself. Six years later, the working-from-home share of paid days in the United States has settled at roughly a quarter to a third, several times the pre-pandemic rate of around 7 percent, according to long-running surveys from the WFH Research project run by economists at Stanford, the University of Chicago, and ITAM. Return-to-office mandates pulled attendance up from the 2021 trough, but they did not restore the five-day office week. Hybrid, not remote, became the equilibrium — and hybrid still means a company that once leased 100,000 square feet now needs perhaps 60,000 to 80,000.

Multiplied across a national office stock measured in billions of square feet, that arithmetic produces one of the largest repricings of a single asset class in modern American history.

## What the "trillion-dollar" number actually measures

Headline estimates of office value destruction range widely, and it is worth understanding why before treating any single figure as fact.

A widely cited working paper by economists Arpit Gupta, Vrinda Mittal, and Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, published through the National Bureau of Economic Research, modeled remote work's effect on office cash flows and lease renewals and projected long-run value declines in the hundreds of billions of dollars for U.S. office alone. Separately, the McKinsey Global Institute estimated that office values across nine major global cities could fall by roughly $800 billion by 2030 in a moderate scenario, and by well over $1 trillion in a more severe one.

Figures approaching $2 trillion generally come from broader framings — global rather than U.S.-only, or including the knock-on effects on retail, hotels, and municipal revenue rather than office buildings in isolation. None of these are audited losses. They are model outputs, sensitive to assumptions about interest rates, lease expiration schedules, and how much space tenants ultimately give back.

What is not modeled is the observable part: buildings that have traded hands at 50 to 80 percent below their previous sale price. Over the past three years, offices in Manhattan, Chicago's Loop, downtown Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington, and St. Louis have all sold at steep discounts to prices paid in the 2014–2019 cycle. Several changed hands for less than the cost of the land beneath them. Those transactions are not projections — they are comparables, and appraisers use them to reprice everything nearby.

## Why vacancy turned into devaluation so slowly, then so fast

Office leases are long. A tenant that decided in 2021 to cut its footprint in half may not have been able to act on that decision until a 2026 expiration. This is the central reason the office correction has unfolded as a slow bleed rather than a crash: the damage arrives one lease expiration at a time.

Three forces then compounded it.

**Vacancy climbed to records.** National office vacancy has hovered around 20 percent, the highest level in the more than four decades Moody's Analytics has tracked the series. Availability — which includes space that is leased but being marketed for sublease — runs several points higher still.

**Financing costs reset.** A building generating the same rent is worth materially less when the discount rate rises. The interest rate cycle that began in 2022 devalued all real estate; office simply had no rent growth to offset it.

**The debt came due.** The Mortgage Bankers Association has estimated that close to $1 trillion of commercial mortgages were scheduled to mature in 2025, with heavy volumes following. Loans written when a tower was 92 percent leased and rates were near zero cannot always be refinanced when it is 65 percent leased and rates are not. Office delinquency rates in commercial mortgage-backed securities climbed into the double digits — exceeding the peaks recorded after the 2008 financial crisis, according to data firm Trepp — and lenders have increasingly chosen extensions, discounted payoffs, or deed-in-lieu handovers rather than forcing sales into a thin market.

## Not one market, but two

The most consistent misreading of this story treats "office" as a single asset. It is not.

Newer, amenity-rich, well-located buildings — the trophy tier — have held occupancy and in several markets have posted record asking rents. Companies shrinking their footprints have frequently upgraded them at the same time, using better space as an argument for coming in. Developers built comparatively little new office during the 2020s, so the supply of genuinely top-tier space is limited.

The pain concentrates in the tier below: 1970s and 1980s commodity towers with deep floor plates, dated systems, single-pane curtain walls, and no realistic capital budget for renovation. Many of these buildings are not temporarily underleased. They are functionally obsolete, and their highest-value use may no longer be as offices at all.

This bifurcation matters for policy, because a citywide vacancy average conceals it. A downtown can post 22 percent vacancy while its best five buildings are full and its worst twenty are effectively empty.

## The municipal squeeze

For city governments, the transmission channel is property tax.

Commercial property is assessed on income. When income falls, assessments follow — sometimes after a lag, often after litigation. In cities where downtown commercial parcels carry an outsized share of the levy, a reassessment cycle can open a structural hole in the operating budget. Boston, which draws roughly 70 percent of its revenue from property taxes and historically taxes commercial property at a higher rate than residential, has drawn particular attention from analysts at the Tufts Center for State Policy Analysis and elsewhere for that concentration. San Francisco, New York, Chicago, and Washington face variations on the same problem.

The knock-on effects are less visible than the budget line but just as real. Downtown lunch counters, dry cleaners, parking operators, and transit agencies were all sized for a five-day commuter population. Transit systems that once covered a large share of operating costs from fares have seen ridership recover unevenly, with weekday peaks flattened even where weekend travel has fully returned.

The pessimistic framing of this is the "urban doom loop": falling values cut revenue, revenue cuts degrade services, degraded services push out residents and employers, and values fall further. It is a coherent risk, and it deserves to be taken seriously. But it is a scenario, not a forecast. Cities are not passive in it, and the evidence of the past two years is that many are acting.

## Conversion: real, growing, and not a cure-all

The obvious answer to empty offices in a country short of housing is to turn one into the other. The obvious answer is also harder than it sounds.

Postwar office towers were designed around large floor plates with deep interior cores — space that is fine for cubicles and impossible for bedrooms, which need windows. Plumbing risers built for a few restrooms per floor must be multiplied for dozens of kitchens and bathrooms. Facades often cannot be opened. Zoning may forbid residential use outright. And the arithmetic only works when the acquisition price is low enough to absorb $200 to $500 per square foot of retrofit cost, which in practice means the seller must accept a deeply discounted price first.

Even so, the pipeline has grown substantially. CBRE and other brokerages have tracked well over 70 million square feet of U.S. office slated for conversion, with completions hitting successive records over the past two years — still only a low single-digit percentage of national inventory, but heavily concentrated in exactly the downtowns that need it.

Policy has moved to close the gap:

- **New York City** created an Office Conversion Accelerator to shepherd projects through permitting, paired it with a state tax exemption for conversions that include affordable units, and passed the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity zoning amendments in late 2024 to widen eligibility.
- **Washington, D.C.** has offered a multiyear tax abatement for downtown residential conversions as part of an explicit downtown population target.
- **Boston** launched a conversion program offering long-term partial property tax abatements to make retrofit math work.
- **Chicago** anchored its LaSalle Street Reimagined initiative on public subsidy tied to affordable housing requirements.
- **Calgary**, outside the U.S. but the most-studied case in North America, committed substantial public funding to a per-square-foot conversion grant and has removed several million square feet of office from its downtown inventory.

A quieter parallel track is demolition. Removing a functionally obsolete building from the inventory improves the market for everything left standing, and in some cases a surface lot with development optionality is worth more than a tower with negative cash flow.

## What to watch next

The office correction is now mature enough that the useful questions have shifted from "how bad" to "how does it resolve."

**Does leasing volume keep recovering?** Leasing activity in major markets has improved from the trough, and several central business districts have posted positive net absorption after years of negative readings. Sustained absorption, more than any price index, is the signal that demand has found its floor.

**How much space gets permanently removed?** Conversion plus demolition is the only mechanism that fixes oversupply structurally. Watch inventory, not just vacancy.

**Do the loans clear?** Extensions bought time; they did not resolve losses. The pace at which distressed office debt is actually written down and recapitalized determines whether the sector's overhang lifts in three years or ten.

**Do downtowns become residential?** The most durable version of the recovery is not offices refilling — it is central business districts becoming central neighborhoods, with a resident population that supports street-level commerce seven days a week rather than five.

That transition is expensive, slow, and unevenly feasible across cities. It is also, in most of the serious proposals now on the table, the actual plan. The trillion-dollar figure describes what was lost on one side of the ledger. What gets built on the other side is still being decided.
